title: Testing a standardised reporting tool (PACT-UK) for pancreatic cancer
official: IMAGINE PACT: Imaging dataset curation for the multicentre validation of PACT-UK (Pancreatic Cancer Reporting Template UK)
summary:
Background and study aims 
Pancreatic cancer is difficult to diagnose and treat. CT scans are used to assess pancreatic tumours and help doctors plan treatment. Inconsistent reporting can make results harder to compare and plan treatment and carry out research. PACT-UK is a national structured reporting tool designed to help radiologists describe pancreatic cancer CT scans in a consistent way.
IMAGINE PACT will assess how consistently radiologists use PACT-UK when reporting pancreatic cancer CT scans across NHS hospitals. The study will assess agreement between different radiologists and consistency when the same radiologist reviews the same scan on two occasions. It will also identify areas where the reporting tool may need refinement or additional training. 

Who can participate?
The study includes adults aged 18 years or over who have had a pancreatic CT scan and a PACT-UK report as part of routine NHS care for suspected or confirmed pancreatic cancer, subject to the study eligibility criteria.
No additional scans, tests or hospital visits are required.
There are two routes into the study:
1. Prospective cohort: NHS patients who meet the eligibility criteria may be approached by the research team and asked to provide written consent.
2. Retrospective cohort: historical cases from the preceding two years may be included where it is not practicable to contact a patient to ask for consent, for example if they have died or cannot be contacted. Patient’s information will only be used in this way where the appropriate NHS approvals are in place, including Section 251 support following advice from the NHS Confidentiality Advisory Group (CAG).

What does the study involve?
IMAGINE PACT uses CT scans and associated PACT-UK structured reports that have already produced as part of routine NHS care. No additional scans, tests, treatments or hospital visits are required.
For the prospective cohort, eligible patients are approached for consent before their study information is accessed.
For the retrospective cohort, historical cases may be identified from routinely held clinical records under the approved Section 251 pathway, where prospective consent is not practicable, for example if they have died or can no longer be contacted. Information from these patients will only be used where the required approvals are in place, including Section 251 support from the Health Research Authority, following advice from the Confidentiality Advisory Group, and where the patient has not opted out. 
For the retrospective cohort, the National Data Opt-Out will be checked and respected in accordance with the approved study arrangements. A study-specific opt-out mechanism is also available. Patients who do not want their information to be included in IMAGINE PACT can contact their local research team/treating team at the participating hospital. The request will be recorded locally and communicated to the study team before information relating to the patient is included. 
Patients can opt out without giving a reason, and the National Data Opt-Out is respected. Details of how to opt out are set out in the study's Fair Processing Notice, available as an attached document.
Before information leaves the participating hospital, identifying details such as name, NHS number and date of birth are replaced with a unique study code. The link between the patient's identity and their code remains securely at the originating hospital and is not shared with the central research team.
Participating radiologists independently review selected pseudonymised CT scans and complete the PACT-UK structured report without seeing other radiologists' reports. The same radiologists repeat the assessment for a subset of scans after a minimum interval of four weeks.
For full details on how information is used and protected, including the current list of participating hospitals and local opt-out contacts, please see the attached IMAGINE PACT Fair Processing Notice.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
There is no expected direct benefit to an individual from taking part or from their information being included. The results may help improve consistency in pancreatic cancer CT reporting across the NHS, which could support refinement of PACT-UK and associated training, clearer communication between doctors and better-informed treatment decisions for future patients. 
No additional procedures are involved, so there are no additional medical risks. 
The main potential risk relates to the use of confidential health information. This is addressed through pseudonymisation, secure research systems, restricted access, retention of the local linkage record at the originating hospital and the approved governance arrangements.

Where is the study run from?
The study is sponsored by The Christie NHS Foundation Trust (UK) and is being carried out in partnership with the Institute of Cancer Research and participating NHS specialist hospitals in England and Scotland.

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
October 2026 to October 2028

Who is funding the study?
Pancreatic Cancer UK

Who is the main contact?
1. Mona Khoo, mona.khoo@nhs.net
2. Dr Ganesh Radhakrishna, g.radhakrishna@nhs.net

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Adults aged 18 years or over at the time of imaging
2. Suspected or confirmed pancreatic neoplasm discussed at a hepatopancreatobiliary (HPB) multidisciplinary team meeting
3. Non-metastatic disease at the time of imaging
4. Contrast-enhanced CT of the pancreas performed as part of routine NHS clinical care*
5. Availability of a completed PACT-UK structured radiology report associated with the imaging study

* MRI scans acquired as part of routine clinical care may additionally be included for dataset curation and secondary objectives but are not eligible for the primary reliability analysis.
Exclusion criteria:
1. Evidence of distant metastatic disease at the time of imaging
2. Imaging studies that are technically inadequate for structured reporting
